Prep now — quick, focused plan and practice for a final-round analyst interview at an M&A boutique:
1) What they want in an analyst (top priorities)
- Technical accuracy and speed on accounting, valuation and modeling basics.
- Clear, structured thinking (one idea at a time).
- Attention to detail and ability to explain numbers without hand-waving.
- Deal awareness: how you thought about past deals, your role, outcomes.
- Fit: stamina, drive, teamwork, client-readiness and polished communication.
2) 20-minute prep checklist (do these now)
- Bring one short story for each: (a) Deal / transaction you worked on, (b) A time you fixed an error or caught a problem, (c) A time you worked under tight deadline with a team. Each story: Situation, Task, Action (what you specifically did), Result (quantify).
- Refresh technicals: three quick calculations to be ready to do on a whiteboard or screen:
- Walk me through a 3-statement linkage and one example of how a change in revenue flows to cash.
- Basic DCF: unlevered free cash flow → discount rate (WACC) → terminal value (exit multiple vs. Gordon growth) → enterprise value → equity value.
- Accretion/dilution: how to test whether an acquisition is accretive to EPS and why.
- Re-read the resume bullets tied to deals — be ready to explain your exact role, deliverables, and an outcome (number, timeline, or client reaction).
- One-minute commercial: why Lincoln International, why M&A, why you now — crisp, specific to their firm (e.g., middle-market focus, sector strengths). Have 2 reasons tied to their firm and one personal motivation.
- Prepare 3 intelligent questions for interviewers (one about deal flow / sectors, one about team structure and promotion path, one about a recent Lincoln deal or market view).
3) Answers to expect and how to structure them
- Tell me about yourself: 60–90 seconds. Structure: current role → highlight 2 relevant deal examples/skills → why M&A at Lincoln (tie to firm).
- Walk me through this deal on your resume: start with context (size, sector), your role (exact tasks and tools), one challenge, and outcome (value created, timing).
- Technical: If asked to solve, speak aloud your assumptions, state steps, and check units at the end (per-share vs. enterprise).
- Behavioral: use STAR and end each answer with a concrete result or what you learned.
4) Mistakes that kill you (and how to avoid)
- Saying “we” when you mean “I” — always name your actions.
- Vague numbers — replace “helped with modeling” with “built 3-statement model and sensitivity table that informed client’s decision to accept a 12% premium.”
- Not asking clarifying questions on technical prompts — pause, clarify the scope, then start.
- Being unprepared to discuss valuation choices (why pick multiples vs. DCF).
5) 10-point quick prep if you have an hour
- Read the interview invite and note participants (send it to me to save).
- Write the three STAR stories and rehearse them aloud.
- Build a 5-minute walkthrough of one full deal on your resume (figures and timeline).
- Practice a DCF walkthrough out loud.
- Practice explaining a cap table adjustment (debt, cash, options).
- Read Lincoln International recent deals (pick 2 public press releases; have one question about each).
- Prepare questions for each interviewer type (junior vs. director vs. partner).
- Mock answers to: “Why Lincoln?” and “Where do you see yourself in 3 years?”
- One-minute deep breath / posture plan for video (camera at eye level, notes on a single sheet).
- Print or have a one-page cheat sheet with bullet facts: your 3 stories, 3 technical points, and your questions.

6) Mock question to start now
"Walk me through a deal you worked on that had a significant valuation challenge. What did you do and what was the outcome?"
